questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum
questions.problem: What is ${\int }_{2}^{6}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral,

$$
{\int }_{2}^{6}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=2,$ and the upper bound is $b=6.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{6-2}{n}=\frac{4}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{6}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(2+i\cdot \frac{4}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(2+\frac{4i}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(2+\frac{4i}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing the Area Bounded by a Curve as a Definite Integral
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13947210/assets/149fd953075c1d9909e036d4935ccd4f17ad1734d86bba4a70254468cd2035d5.png)

For the function $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x+2$ shown above, what is the expression for the area $A$ as a definite integral?
questions.worked_solution:
We want to express the area $A$ between the function $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x+2$ and the $x$-axis, between $x=0$ and $x=3.$

This can be expressed as the definite integral of $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x+2$ between the lower limit $x=0$ and the upper limit $x=3,$ as follows:

$$
A={\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{2}-2x+2)\,\text{d}x
$$

questions.problem:
What is ${\int }_{1}^{4}9{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{1}^{4}9{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[9($
{{field-1}}
$)^{\,3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}]$
questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{4}9{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=9{x}^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=1$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{4-1}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}9{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(1+\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[9{(1+\frac{3i}{n})}^{\,3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum as a Definite Integral
questions.problem:
Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that

$$
{\int }_{2}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[({2}^{\,2+3k/n}+1)\cdot \frac{3}{n}].
$$

$\,f(x)=$
{{field-1}} $\,$ and 
$\,b=$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=2.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{3}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{3}{n}=\frac{b-2}{n}\,⟹\,b=5.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=2+\frac{3k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})={2}^{\,{x}_{k}}+1.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{2}^{5}({2}^{x}+1)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[({2}^{\,2+3k/n}+1)\cdot \frac{3}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$
f(x)={2}^{x}+1\,\text{and}\,b=5.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Right Riemann Sum
questions.problem:
What is ${\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[$
{{field-1}}
$\cdot \frac{3}{n}]$
questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\sqrt{x+1},$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(0+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[\sqrt{(\frac{3i}{n})+1}\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[\,\sqrt{\frac{3i}{n}+1}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$
